title: Measuring Transpiration Rate
subtitle: The potometer practical
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: Conduct a practical investigation to demonstrate the effect of an environmental factor on the rate of transpiration
lessonIntent: Students can use a potometer to demonstrate the effect of one environmental factor on transpiration, calculate rates, and evaluate validity, reliability and accuracy.
examSkill: Convert bubble readings to rates (distance ÷ time) before comparing. Unequal observation times are acceptable when rates are normalised; evaluate whether leaks, water storage/use or changing conditions could bias treatments differently.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, measuring transpiration with a potometer. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Catching invisible water loss
scenes.body: You can’t see water leaving a leaf, but you can watch water entering the plant. A potometer turns it into a moving bubble.
scenes.callout: How can a device that tracks water going in tell us about water going out?
scenes.caption: A potometer measures water uptake, a stand-in for transpiration.

voiceover.text: You can't see water leaving a leaf. But every drop the leaves lose has to be replaced by water drawn into the stem. A potometer turns that invisible flow into a tiny air bubble moving along a scale, which you can time with a stopwatch and a ruler. But here's the catch. It measures water going in, not water going out. So how can it tell us about transpiration, and what does that assumption cost us in accuracy?

scenes.heading: The potometer method
scenes.body: As the shoot transpires, it draws water in, and an air bubble moves along a graduated tube.

bullets.text: Cut a leafy shoot under water, so air can’t enter the xylem.
Seal it airtight into the potometer and add one air bubble.
Time how far the bubble moves in a set period.
Rate of water uptake = distance ÷ time.

scenes.caption: The bubble moves 18 mm in 6 min: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 mm per minute.

voiceover.text: Here's how it works. First, cut a leafy shoot under water, so that no air gets into the xylem and breaks the water column. Then seal it airtight into the potometer, and introduce a single air bubble into the graduated tube. As the shoot transpires, it draws water up to replace what it loses, and the bubble moves along the tube towards the shoot. You time how far it travels. Here it moves eighteen millimetres in six minutes. So the rate of water uptake is distance divided by time, eighteen divided by six, which is three millimetres per minute.

scenes.heading: A fair test for one factor
scenes.body: Change only the chosen factor, here wind, and keep everything else the same.

bullets.text: Independent variable: wind (fan off, then fan on).
Dependent variable: rate of water uptake (mm of bubble movement per minute).
Controlled: same shoot/leaf area, temperature, light, humidity and potometer; observation times may differ if both readings are converted to rates.
A higher rate with the fan demonstrates that wind increases transpiration.

scenes.callout: Change one factor; hold the rest.
scenes.caption: Still air 3 mm/min; with a fan 8 mm/min.

voiceover.text: To test one factor, here wind, change only that factor. The independent variable is wind, with the fan off then on. The dependent variable is the rate of water uptake, so convert each bubble movement to distance per unit time. Keep the shoot, leaf area, temperature, light, humidity and apparatus the same. The two observation times do not have to be identical if both results are normalised to rates. In this example, eighteen millimetres in six minutes is three millimetres per minute, and forty millimetres in five minutes is eight millimetres per minute.

scenes.heading: Validity, reliability and accuracy
scenes.body: A good result is one you can defend.

bullets.text: Validity: only the chosen factor changed, so the result really tests it.
Reliability: repeats that agree closely, averaged.
Accuracy: uptake slightly overstates transpiration; some water is used in photosynthesis and turgor.
Other issues: leaks, a dissolving bubble, temperature drifting.

scenes.callout: Uptake is a close proxy for transpiration, not an exact one.
scenes.caption: Three repeats with the fan average 8 mm per minute.

proxy.text: Some water taken up is used in photosynthesis and turgor, so uptake slightly overstates transpiration.

voiceover.text: How much should we trust the result? Check three things. Validity means only the chosen factor changed, so the result genuinely tests wind. A fan can also cool the shoot, so temperature has to be watched. Reliability means repeating the measurement. Here are three runs with the fan, and because they're close together, the average of eight millimetres per minute can be trusted. Accuracy is the subtle one. The potometer measures water uptake, and a little of that water is used in photosynthesis or kept in cells for turgor, so uptake slightly overstates transpiration. Leaks, a dissolving bubble or a drifting temperature can also affect accuracy.

scenes.heading: The words you need
scenes.body: Five terms for the potometer practical.

bullets.text: Potometer: measures the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, by timing an air bubble along a graduated tube.
Independent variable: the one factor deliberately changed (wind, light or humidity).
Dependent variable: the rate of water uptake, used as a measure of transpiration.
Controlled variable: a factor kept constant so the test is fair (valid).
Reliability: how consistent results are when repeated; improved by repeats and averaging.

scenes.callout: A potometer measures uptake, not transpiration directly.
scenes.caption: Potometer, independent, dependent and controlled variables, reliability.

voiceover.text: Let's lock in the terms. A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, by timing an air bubble along a graduated tube. The independent variable is the one factor you deliberately change, like wind, light or humidity. The dependent variable is the rate of water uptake, which we use as a measure of transpiration. A controlled variable is kept constant, so the test is fair, or valid. And reliability is how consistent the results are when you repeat them, which you improve by repeating and averaging.

scenes.heading: Analyse the potometer results
scenes.question: A potometer bubble moves 18 mm in 6 minutes with no fan, and 40 mm in 5 minutes with a fan. Calculate both rates, state what the comparison shows, and explain why the rate slightly overstates transpiration.
scenes.coachNote: The times differ, so convert both readings to rates before comparing.
steps: 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.7, so wind increased the rate about 2.7 times in this shoot.
Mechanism: the fan strips away the humid boundary layer, keeping the vapour gradient steep.
Limitation: water uptake is only a proxy for transpiration. Storage, metabolism, leaks or changing conditions may affect treatments differently, so do not assume the error cancels.
scenes.caption: 3 mm/min without the fan, 8 mm/min with it: about 2.7 times faster.

voiceover.text: Let's analyse the data. With no fan the bubble moved eighteen millimetres in six minutes, and with the fan forty millimetres in five minutes. Because the times differ, compare rates rather than raw distances. Eighteen divided by six is three millimetres per minute; forty divided by five is eight. Wind increased the measured uptake rate about two point seven times in this shoot. The mechanism is that moving air reduces the humid boundary layer. But evaluate the method carefully: water uptake is only a proxy for transpiration, and water storage or use, leaks, or changing conditions could affect the two treatments differently. Do not simply claim the limitation cancels equally.

scenes.heading: A potometer measures transpiration directly?
scenes.body: Wrong: a potometer measures transpiration directly.
scenes.secondary: Right: it measures the rate of water uptake. Almost all of that water is transpired, so uptake is a close proxy, but a little is used in photosynthesis and to keep cells turgid.
scenes.callout: Call it water uptake, then say it slightly overstates transpiration.
scenes.caption: A potometer measures water uptake, a close but not exact proxy.

voiceover.text: Here's the precise point examiners love. A potometer does not measure transpiration directly. It measures the rate of water uptake. We assume almost all the water taken up is lost by transpiration, so uptake is a close stand-in. But a small amount is used in photosynthesis, and some is kept in cells to keep them turgid. So uptake slightly overstates transpiration. That's a known limit on accuracy, not a mistake in your method.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Why must the leafy shoot be cut under water and sealed airtight into the potometer?
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause: what would air do to the water column?
answerSteps: Cutting in air lets air enter the xylem, breaking the continuous water column.
A broken column can’t transmit tension, so the shoot draws up little or no water.
An airtight seal stops leaks, so the bubble moves only because of the shoot’s uptake.
Answer: both keep the measurement valid.
scenes.caption: Air in the xylem breaks the column; leaks give false readings.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Why must the shoot be cut under water, and sealed airtight into the potometer? Pause, and think about what air would do to the water column. OK. If you cut the shoot in air, air gets into the xylem and breaks the continuous water column. Cohesion can't pass the pull along a broken column, so the shoot draws up little or no water. And an airtight seal stops leaks, so the bubble only moves because of the shoot's uptake. Both keep the measurement valid.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: A potometer measures water uptake, a close proxy for transpiration.
Cut the shoot under water and seal it airtight.
Rate = distance the bubble moves ÷ time.
Change one factor; control the rest; repeat and average.
Uptake slightly overstates transpiration: some water is used, not lost.
scenes.finalPrompt: Potometer data? Convert to rates before you compare.
scenes.caption: Uptake as a proxy, rate = distance ÷ time, fair tests and repeats.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. A potometer measures water uptake, which is a close stand-in for transpiration. Cut the shoot under water, and seal it airtight. The rate is the distance the bubble moves divided by the time. Change one factor, control the rest, and repeat and average. And remember that uptake slightly overstates transpiration, because some water is used rather than lost. Next lesson, we'll look inside the leaf, stem and root.
